# The Great Transition: Java EE to Jakarta EE

### 1. What It Is and Why It Exists
For nearly two decades, the standard enterprise server-side platform for Java was **Java 2 Platform, Enterprise Edition (J2EE)** and later **Java Platform, Enterprise Edition (Java EE)**, stewarded originally by Sun Microsystems and subsequently Oracle. Enterprise Java specifications—such as Servlets, JavaServer Pages (JSP), Enterprise JavaBeans (EJB), Java Persistence API (JPA), and JAX-RS—governed billions of dollars in global commerce, banking, and government infrastructure. All of these APIs lived within the venerable `javax.*` package namespace (e.g., `javax.servlet.http.HttpServlet`, `javax.persistence.Entity`).

In 2017, Oracle made the historic decision to open-source the entirety of Java EE to the vendor-neutral **Eclipse Foundation**, where the community rebranded the platform as **Jakarta EE**.
However, while Oracle donated the source code and Technology Compatibility Kits (TCKs), Oracle retained the proprietary commercial trademark on the name **"Java"**. Under the legal agreement between Oracle and the Eclipse Foundation:
1. The Eclipse Foundation could not evolve any APIs under the `javax.*` namespace.
2. The `javax.*` package namespace was permanently frozen at the Java EE 8 feature level.
3. To innovate and release newer versions, the community had to execute the **"Big Bang" namespace migration**: changing every enterprise package name from `javax.*` to `jakarta.*` (e.g., `javax.servlet.*` became `jakarta.servlet.*`).

This shift caused the biggest backward-compatibility break in Java history, requiring modern servlet containers (Apache Tomcat 10+, Eclipse Jetty 11+, WildFly 27+) to adopt the new `jakarta.*` namespace.

**Real-World Analogy:**
Imagine an international telecom provider that operated country codes under the brand name `"JavaPhone"` using dialed prefix `+99` (`javax.*`). When the company was donated to a public global foundation, the original owner retained the trademark `"JavaPhone"`. The foundation renamed the network to `"JakartaPhone"` and updated the international calling prefix to `+77` (`jakarta.*`). Cell towers built before the handover (Tomcat 9) only accept `+99` calls. Modern towers (Tomcat 10+) only accept `+77` calls.

---

### 2. Prerequisites
- **Packages and Namespaces (Topic 18)**: Understanding how package names uniquely define types.
- **JPMS and Modules (Topic 60)**: Understanding modular boundaries and namespace isolation.

---

### 3. Syntax Breakdown

#### 3.1 The Import Statement Transformation
The most immediate syntactic consequence of the transition is in import statements across every enterprise web application:
```java
// LEGACY (Java EE 8 / Tomcat 9 and older):
import javax.servlet.ServletException;
import javax.servlet.http.HttpServlet;
import javax.servlet.http.HttpServletRequest;
import javax.servlet.http.HttpServletResponse;

// MODERN (Jakarta EE 10 / Tomcat 10.1+ / Tomcat 11):
import jakarta.servlet.ServletException;
import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServlet;
import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletRequest;
import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletResponse;
```

#### 3.2 XML Schema Namespace Changes in `web.xml`
In addition to Java source imports, deployment descriptors updated their XML schemas:
- **Legacy Java EE 8 (`web.xml`)**:
  `xmlns="http://xmlns.jcp.org/xml/ns/javaee"`
- **Modern Jakarta EE 10 (`web.xml`)**:
  `xmlns="https://jakarta.ee/xml/ns/jakartaee"` (version `"6.0"`)

#### 3.3 Server & Container Compatibility Rules
- **Tomcat 9.0.x**: Supports Servlet 4.0 / Java EE 8 (`javax.*` namespace). Runs on Java 8+.
- **Tomcat 10.1.x** (Current Stable): Supports Servlet 6.0 / Jakarta EE 10 (`jakarta.*` namespace). Requires Java 11+.
- **Tomcat 11.0.x** (Cutting Edge): Supports Servlet 6.1 / Jakarta EE 11 (`jakarta.*` namespace). Requires Java 17+.

---

### 4. Code Examples

#### Example 1: Programmatic Detection of the Active Container Namespace
The following example inspects the active runtime classpath, verifying the presence of the modern `jakarta.*` servlet API:

```java
public class NamespaceTransitionInspectorDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== The Great Transition: Java EE to Jakarta EE ===");

        System.out.println("1. 1999 - 2017: Java EE (Sun Microsystems -> Oracle Corporation)");
        System.out.println("   Package Namespace: javax.* (e.g. javax.servlet.http.HttpServlet)");

        System.out.println("2. 2017: Oracle donates Java EE to Eclipse Foundation.");
        System.out.println("   Oracle retains 'Java' trademark; requires namespace migration.");

        System.out.println("3. 2019: Jakarta EE 8 released (fully identical to Java EE 8, still javax.*).");

        System.out.println("4. 2020: Jakarta EE 9 'Big Bang' migration (namespace permanently switched to jakarta.*).");

        System.out.println("5. Modern Production: Jakarta EE 10 / 11 (Servlet 6.0/6.1, Tomcat 10.1/11).");

        try {
            Class<?> servletClass = Class.forName("jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServlet");
            System.out.println("\nActive Servlet API Detected: " + servletClass.getName());
            System.out.println("Namespace: 'jakarta.*' (Modern Jakarta EE Container verified)");
        } catch (ClassNotFoundException e) {
            System.out.println("\nServlet API not on standalone boot classpath (Standard in Java SE runtime)");
        }

        System.out.println("Namespace transition inspection completed successfully.");
    }
}
```

```text

   Package Namespace: javax.* (e.g. javax.servlet.http.HttpServlet)
2. 2017: Oracle donates Java EE to Eclipse Foundation.
   Oracle retains 'Java' trademark; requires namespace migration.
3. 2019: Jakarta EE 8 released (fully identical to Java EE 8, still javax.*).
4. 2020: Jakarta EE 9 'Big Bang' migration (namespace permanently switched to jakarta.*).
5. Modern Production: Jakarta EE 10 / 11 (Servlet 6.0/6.1, Tomcat 10.1/11).

Active Servlet API Detected: jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServlet
Namespace: 'jakarta.*' (Modern Jakarta EE Container verified)
Namespace transition inspection completed successfully.
```

#### Example 2: Realistic Application — Server Compatibility Matrix Evaluator
In enterprise migration audits, software architects evaluate which servlet container versions and Java versions can host target enterprise workloads:

```java
import java.util.List;

public class ServerCompatibilityMatrixApp {
    record CompatibilityEntry(
            String serverName,
            String serverVersion,
            String jakartaVersion,
            String servletSpec,
            String namespace,
            int minimumJavaVersion
    ) {}

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Starting Server Compatibility Matrix Evaluator...\n");

        List<CompatibilityEntry> matrix = List.of(
                new CompatibilityEntry("Apache Tomcat", "9.0.x", "Java EE 8", "Servlet 4.0", "javax.*", 8),
                new CompatibilityEntry("Apache Tomcat", "10.1.x", "Jakarta EE 10", "Servlet 6.0", "jakarta.*", 11),
                new CompatibilityEntry("Apache Tomcat", "11.0.x", "Jakarta EE 11", "Servlet 6.1", "jakarta.*", 17),
                new CompatibilityEntry("Eclipse Jetty", "11.x", "Jakarta EE 9", "Servlet 5.0", "jakarta.*", 11),
                new CompatibilityEntry("Eclipse Jetty", "12.x", "Jakarta EE 10/11", "Servlet 6.0", "jakarta.*", 17),
                new CompatibilityEntry("WildFly", "30.x+", "Jakarta EE 10", "Full Profile", "jakarta.*", 17),
                new CompatibilityEntry("Eclipse GlassFish", "7.0.x", "Jakarta EE 10", "Full Profile", "jakarta.*", 17)
        );

        System.out.printf("%-18s | %-10s | %-15s | %-12s | %-10s | Min Java%n",
                "Server", "Version", "EE Level", "Servlet Spec", "Namespace");
        System.out.println("-".repeat(82));

        for (CompatibilityEntry entry : matrix) {
            System.out.printf("%-18s | %-10s | %-15s | %-12s | %-10s | Java %d+%n",
                    entry.serverName(), entry.serverVersion(), entry.jakartaVersion(),
                    entry.servletSpec(), entry.namespace(), entry.minimumJavaVersion());
        }

        System.out.println("\nRule: Any application compiled against 'jakarta.*' WILL NOT run on Tomcat 9.");
        System.out.println("Rule: Any application compiled against 'javax.*' WILL NOT run on Tomcat 10+ (without byte-code migration).");
        System.out.println("Server compatibility evaluation completed successfully.");
    }

```

**Expected Output:**
```text

Apache Tomcat      | 10.1.x     | Jakarta EE 10   | Servlet 6.0  | jakarta.*  | Java 11+
Apache Tomcat      | 11.0.x     | Jakarta EE 11   | Servlet 6.1  | jakarta.*  | Java 17+
Eclipse Jetty      | 11.x       | Jakarta EE 9    | Servlet 5.0  | jakarta.*  | Java 11+
Eclipse Jetty      | 12.x       | Jakarta EE 10/11 | Servlet 6.0  | jakarta.*  | Java 17+
WildFly            | 30.x+      | Jakarta EE 10   | Full Profile | jakarta.*  | Java 17+
Eclipse GlassFish  | 7.0.x      | Jakarta EE 10   | Full Profile | jakarta.*  | Java 17+

Rule: Any application compiled against 'jakarta.*' WILL NOT run on Tomcat 9.
Rule: Any application compiled against 'javax.*' WILL NOT run on Tomcat 10+ (without byte-code migration).
Server compatibility evaluation completed successfully.
```

---

### 5. Step-by-Step Execution Trace
1. When a developer compiles a modern servlet class, `javac` checks dependencies against `tools/apache-tomcat-10.1.61/lib/servlet-api.jar`.
2. The compiler resolves symbol `jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServlet`.
3. The resulting bytecode encodes method signatures pointing directly to the `Ljakarta/servlet/http/HttpServlet;` descriptor.
4. When deployed to Tomcat 10.1, the Catalina classloader matches the `jakarta.*` bytecode types with its own container libraries without classloading mismatches.

---

### 6. Common Mistakes & Error Diagnosis

#### Pitfall 1: Deploying a `javax.*` WAR to Tomcat 10+
Deploying an old Java EE 8 application compiled with `import javax.servlet.*` onto Apache Tomcat 10 or 11:
- **Consequence**: The container starts, but throws `java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError: javax/servlet/http/HttpServlet` or completely ignores `@WebServlet` annotations.
- **Fix**: Either update source code imports to `jakarta.*` and recompile, or run the Apache Tomcat Migration Tool for Jakarta EE (`jakartaee-migration-*.jar`) to rewrite class bytecode inside the WAR archive.

#### Pitfall 2: Mixing `javax.*` and `jakarta.*` Dependencies
A project imports `jakarta.servlet-api` version 6.0, but transitively brings in an old library depending on `javax.servlet:servlet-api:2.5`:
- **Consequence**: Compilation succeeds, but passing request or response objects between libraries throws `ClassCastException` because `javax.servlet.ServletRequest` and `jakarta.servlet.ServletRequest` are distinct types.
- **Fix**: Exclude legacy `javax.*` transitive dependencies in `pom.xml` or `build.gradle`.

---

### 7. Best Practices & When NOT to Use
- **Do**: Build all new enterprise and web projects targeting **Jakarta EE 10 or 11** with Apache Tomcat 10.1+ or 11+.
- **Do**: Update Maven dependencies to the official coordinates:
  `jakarta.servlet:jakarta.servlet-api:6.0.0` (scope: `provided`).
- **Don't**: Do not initiate new production projects on Java EE 8 / Tomcat 9 unless supporting legacy un-upgradable legacy vendor infrastructure.

---

### 8. Version Notes
- **Java EE 8 (2017)**: Last Oracle release under `javax.*`.
- **Jakarta EE 8 (2019)**: First Eclipse Foundation release; identical to Java EE 8, still using `javax.*`.
- **Jakarta EE 9 (2020)**: Milestone release switching namespace to `jakarta.*` (Servlet 5.0).
- **Jakarta EE 10 (2022)**: Modern baseline release (Servlet 6.0, Java 11+ required).
- **Jakarta EE 11 (2024+)**: Latest release (Servlet 6.1, Java 17/21 LTS baseline).

---

### 9. Summary Cheat Sheet

| Platform | Namespace | Servlet Version | Primary Tomcat Version | Minimum Java |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Java EE 8** | `javax.*` | Servlet 4.0 | Apache Tomcat 9.0.x | Java 8 |
| **Jakarta EE 9** | `jakarta.*` | Servlet 5.0 | Apache Tomcat 10.0.x (EOL) | Java 8 |
| **Jakarta EE 10** | `jakarta.*` | Servlet 6.0 | **Apache Tomcat 10.1.x (Stable)** | **Java 11+** |
| **Jakarta EE 11** | `jakarta.*` | Servlet 6.1 | Apache Tomcat 11.0.x | Java 17+ |

---

### 10. Exercises with Hidden Solutions

#### Exercise 1: Identify Missing Dependency
A developer writes `@WebServlet("/test")` and imports `jakarta.servlet.annotation.WebServlet`, but Maven throws `package jakarta.servlet.annotation does not exist`. What dependency is missing from `pom.xml`?

<details>
<summary>View Solution</summary>

```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>jakarta.servlet</groupId>
    <artifactId>jakarta.servlet-api</artifactId>
    <version>6.0.0</version>
    <scope>provided</scope>
</dependency>
```
</details>

#### Exercise 2: Why Scope Provided?
Why should `jakarta.servlet-api` be given scope `<scope>provided</scope>` in web application projects?

<details>
<summary>View Solution</summary>

```text
Solution:
The Servlet API interfaces are provided at runtime by the web container (such as Apache Tomcat in 'lib/servlet-api.jar'). If the application bundles its own servlet-api.jar inside 'WEB-INF/lib', classloader conflicts and ClassCastExceptions will occur when Tomcat attempts to load its own container implementation.
```
</details>

---

markdownContent:
# Apache Tomcat & The WAR Structure

### 1. What It Is and Why It Exists
Java desktop applications are packaged as Java Archives (`.jar`) and executed by invoking `public static void main(String[] args)`. However, enterprise web applications do not contain a `main` method. Instead, they are packaged as **Web Archives (`.war`)** and deployed inside a **Web Container** (or **Servlet Container**) such as **Apache Tomcat**.

The Web Container manages the entire application lifecycle:
- **Network Listening**: Listens on TCP port 8080 or 8443, accepting incoming HTTP client socket connections.
- **Protocol Decoding**: Parses raw HTTP request bytes into strongly typed `HttpServletRequest` objects.
- **Thread Management**: Dispatches worker threads from an internal thread pool to process concurrent requests.
- **Servlet Lifecycle**: Instantiates servlets, invokes `init()`, calls `service()` for every request, and calls `destroy()` on shutdown.
- **Security & Sandboxing**: Enforces web security constraints and isolates applications from one another.

To run inside a container, an application must adhere strictly to the standardized **WAR Directory Structure**.

**Real-World Analogy:**
Think of a major international airport terminal. The terminal building, air traffic control towers, runways, baggage conveyors, and jet bridges represent **Apache Tomcat**. The airlines and their airplanes represent individual **WAR Web Applications**. An airline does not build its own private runways or radar towers; it parks its plane at a designated gate (**Context Path**, e.g., `/handbook-demo`), plugs into the airport's pre-existing jet bridges and power lines (**Connectors**), and lets the terminal manage passenger boarding.

---

### 2. Prerequisites
- **Build Tools and Packaging (Topic 62)**: Understanding how Maven packages JAR/WAR files.
- **Jakarta EE Transition (Topic 63)**: Knowing that Tomcat 10.1+ requires `jakarta.servlet.*`.
- **HTTP Fundamentals (Topic 64)**: Understanding HTTP requests, responses, and headers.

---

### 3. Syntax Breakdown

#### 3.1 The Canonical WAR Directory Layout
A `.war` file is a standard ZIP archive with a mandatory internal hierarchy defined by the Servlet Specification:
```text
my-web-app.war
├── index.html                   <- Public: Directly accessible by web clients
├── favicon.ico
├── css/
│   └── styles.css               <- Public static asset: http://host/app/css/styles.css
├── js/
│   └── bundle.js
└── WEB-INF/                     <- PRIVATE & SECURE: Container strictly blocks client access!
    ├── web.xml                  <- Deployment Descriptor (configuration, servlet mappings)
    ├── classes/                 <- Compiled application .class files
    │   └── com/example/web/
    │       └── MyServlet.class
    └── lib/                     <- Third-party library JARs (e.g., sqlite-jdbc.jar)
        └── my-library.jar
```
- **Public Root**: Any file outside `WEB-INF` is directly addressable by client browsers (e.g., `GET /css/styles.css`).
- **`WEB-INF/`**: **Strictly private**. The web container's HTTP connector is legally required to reject any direct client request to `http://host/app/WEB-INF/...` with HTTP `404 Not Found`.
- **`WEB-INF/classes/`**: Target directory where `javac` or Maven outputs compiled `.class` files.
- **`WEB-INF/lib/`**: Contains `.jar` libraries bundled specifically with this application.

#### 3.2 Apache Tomcat Catalina Internal Architecture
Tomcat organizes its processing engine as a nested hierarchy in `conf/server.xml`:
1. `Server`: Represents the entire running Tomcat JVM process.
2. `Service`: Groups one or more network connectors with an execution engine.
3. `Connector`: Listens on network ports (e.g., HTTP/1.1 on port `8080`, AJP on port `8009`).
4. `Engine`: Coordinates request routing across virtual hosts.
5. `Host`: Represents a virtual host or domain name (default: `localhost` with `appBase="webapps"`).
6. `Context`: Represents an individual web application deployed at a specific URI context path (e.g., `/handbook-demo`).

---

### 4. Code Examples

#### Example 1: Programmatic WAR Structure & Security Boundary Validator
The following example simulates inspecting a deployment archive, verifying the presence of required deployment boundaries and public vs private asset separation:

```java
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

public class WarStructureValidatorDemo {
    record WarEntry(String path, boolean isDirectory, long size) {}

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Java Web Archive (WAR) Structure Validator ===");

        List<WarEntry> warManifest = List.of(
                new WarEntry("index.html", false, 1024),
                new WarEntry("css/styles.css", false, 2048),
                new WarEntry("WEB-INF/", true, 0),
                new WarEntry("WEB-INF/web.xml", false, 512),
                new WarEntry("WEB-INF/classes/", true, 0),
                new WarEntry("WEB-INF/classes/com/handbook/web/LifecycleServlet.class", false, 4096),
                new WarEntry("WEB-INF/lib/", true, 0),
                new WarEntry("WEB-INF/lib/sqlite-jdbc-3.49.1.0.jar", false, 14000000)
        );

        boolean hasWebInf = false;
        boolean hasWebXml = false;
        boolean hasClasses = false;
        List<String> publicAssets = new ArrayList<>();

        for (WarEntry entry : warManifest) {
            String p = entry.path();
            if (p.startsWith("WEB-INF/")) {
                hasWebInf = true;
                if (p.equals("WEB-INF/web.xml")) hasWebXml = true;
                if (p.startsWith("WEB-INF/classes/")) hasClasses = true;
            } else {
                publicAssets.add(p);
            }
        }

        System.out.println("1. Security Boundary Check:");
        System.out.println("   WEB-INF Root Present:    " + hasWebInf);
        System.out.println("   web.xml Deployment Desk: " + hasWebXml);
        System.out.println("   Compiled Bytecode Area:  " + hasClasses);

        System.out.println("\n2. Direct Client-Accessible Assets (" + publicAssets.size() + "):");
        for (String asset : publicAssets) {
            System.out.println("   - /" + asset);
        }

        System.out.println("\n3. Protected Internal Assets (Clients cannot request directly):");
        System.out.println("   - /WEB-INF/* is strictly blocked by Web Container HTTP connectors.");
        System.out.println("WAR structure validation completed successfully.");
    }
}

---

### 5. Step-by-Step Execution Trace
1. When a `.war` file is dropped into Tomcat's `webapps/` folder (or deployed via Maven), Tomcat's Host monitor detects the file.
2. Tomcat creates an expanded directory in `webapps/handbook-demo/`.
3. Tomcat creates a dedicated child `WebappClassLoader` for the application, ensuring that classes in `WEB-INF/classes` and JARs in `WEB-INF/lib` take precedence over common server libraries (child-first classloading).
4. Tomcat parses `WEB-INF/web.xml` and scans for `@WebServlet` annotations.
5. The application context path is registered at `/handbook-demo`.
6. Client requests to `http://localhost:8080/handbook-demo/status` are routed by the Catalina Connector through Engine $\to$ Host $\to$ Context $\to$ Servlet.

---

### 6. Common Mistakes & Error Diagnosis

#### Pitfall 1: Placing JSP or Private Files in the Public Root
Placing sensitive business logic templates or database connection configurations outside `WEB-INF`:
- **Consequence**: Any user can type `http://localhost:8080/handbook-demo/config.properties` in their browser and download sensitive configuration files directly!
- **Fix**: Always place internal configuration, templates, and view JSPs inside `WEB-INF/` (e.g., `WEB-INF/views/`).

#### Pitfall 2: Bundling `servlet-api.jar` in `WEB-INF/lib`
Including the servlet API inside the application's `WEB-INF/lib/` directory:
- **Consequence**: Violates the Servlet Specification. Tomcat refuses to load the duplicate API or throws `ClassCastException`.
- **Fix**: In Maven `pom.xml`, mark the servlet API dependency as `<scope>provided</scope>`.

---

### 7. Best Practices & When NOT to Use
- **Do**: Follow the standard Maven webapp layout (`src/main/webapp/WEB-INF/web.xml`).
- **Do**: Name your WAR archive carefully: `ROOT.war` maps to the root context path (`/`), while `myapp.war` maps to `/myapp`.
- **Don't**: Do not edit files inside Tomcat's `work/` or `temp/` directories; these are ephemeral cache directories managed exclusively by the container.

---

### 8. Version Notes
- **Java Servlet 2.2**: Introduced the standardized WAR structure.
- **Servlet 3.0**: Made `web.xml` optional via annotation scanning (`@WebServlet`).
- **Servlet 6.0 (Jakarta EE 10 / Tomcat 10.1+)**: XML schema updated to `https://jakarta.ee/xml/ns/jakartaee`.

---

### 9. Summary Cheat Sheet

| WAR Directory | Visibility | Contents |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `/` (Root) | **Public** | Static HTML, CSS, JS, images |
| `/WEB-INF/` | **Private** | Protected from direct client HTTP requests |
| `/WEB-INF/web.xml` | Server Only | Deployment descriptor configuration |
| `/WEB-INF/classes/`| Server Only | Compiled `.class` files |
| `/WEB-INF/lib/` | Server Only | Third-party dependency `.jar` files |

---

### 10. Exercises with Hidden Solutions

#### Exercise 1: Identify Public vs Private
If an application has files `index.html` in the root and `secret.jsp` inside `WEB-INF/views/secret.jsp`, can a browser request `http://localhost:8080/app/WEB-INF/views/secret.jsp`?

<details>
<summary>View Solution</summary>

```text
Solution:
NO. The web container strictly blocks any HTTP request matching /WEB-INF/* with HTTP 404 Not Found. To render secret.jsp, an internal Java Servlet must forward the request on the server side using RequestDispatcher.forward().
```
</details>

#### Exercise 2: Map to Root Context
How do you deploy a WAR file in Apache Tomcat so that it responds directly to `http://localhost:8080/` without any path prefix?

<details>
<summary>View Solution</summary>

```text
Solution:
Name the WAR archive 'ROOT.war' and place it in the 'webapps/' directory (or configure a Context with path="" in conf/server.xml).
```
</details>

---

# JSP Architecture & Translation Lifecycle ### 1. What It Is and Why It Exists Writing HTML markup by concatenating Java Strings inside an `HttpServlet` (e.g. `out.println("...")`) is tedious, unmaintainable, and prone to syntax bugs. **Jakarta Pages (formerly JavaServer Pages / JSP)** was created to invert this model: allowing web developers to write standard HTML markup with embedded server-side Java expressions and tags. Under the hood, **JSP is not an interpreted scripting language**. A JSP file is an uncompiled template that the container (via the Jasper compiler in Apache Tomcat) translates into a standard Java Servlet source file (`.java`), compiles into bytecode (`.class`), and executes identically to any other compiled servlet. **Real-World Analogy:** Imagine an architectural blueprint written in shorthand notes by a draftsperson. Before construction begins, a specialized engineering computer (**Jasper compiler**) automatically reads the shorthand notes, converts them into a comprehensive engineering CAD drawing (**translated Java Servlet source**), and generates machine code for the robotic assembly line (**compiled bytecode**). The construction robot only ever executes the final machine instructions. --- ### 2. Prerequisites - **Apache Tomcat & WAR Structure (Topic 65)**: Understanding `WEB-INF/` and web application deployment. - **Servlet Lifecycle & Architecture (Topic 66)**: Understanding `init()`, `service()`, and `destroy()`. --- ### 3. Syntax Breakdown #### 3.1 The Two Phases of a JSP Lifecycle 1. **Translation & Compilation Phase (Build Time / First Request)**: - Jasper checks if the `.jsp` file has been modified since the last compile. - Translates `page.jsp` into `page_jsp.java` (extending `HttpJspBase`). - Invokes `javac` to produce `page_jsp.class`. 2. **Request Processing Phase (Runtime)**: - Loads `page_jsp.class` into memory. - Executes `jspInit()` once. - For every incoming client request, invokes `_jspService(HttpServletRequest, HttpServletResponse)`. - On shutdown, invokes `jspDestroy()`. #### 3.2 Anatomy of the Translated `_jspService()` Method ```java // What Tomcat actually compiles behind your JSP: public final class index_jsp extends org.apache.jasper.runtime.HttpJspBase { public void _jspService(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response) throws IOException, ServletException { JspFactory _jspxFactory = JspFactory.getDefaultFactory(); PageContext pageContext = _jspxFactory.getPageContext(this, request, response, null, true, 8192, true); ServletContext application = pageContext.getServletContext(); HttpSession session = pageContext.getSession(); JspWriter out = pageContext.getOut(); // Template text written as raw socket bytes: out.write("\n\n"); // Scriptlets placed directly into method body: String user = request.getParameter("name"); // Expressions wrapped in out.print(): out.print(user != null ? user : "Guest"); out.write("\n"); } } ``` --- ### 4. Runnable Code Examples #### Example 1: Jasper JSP Translation Simulator (Basic) Demonstrates how raw JSP syntax elements (comments, scriptlets, expressions, template text) are deconstructed into a Java Servlet class. ```java package com.handbook.web; public class JspTranslationInspectorDemo { public static String translateJspSnippet(String jspText) { StringBuilder javaSource = new StringBuilder(); javaSource.append("// Translated by Jasper JSP Engine\n"); javaSource.append("public final class HelloJsp extends org.apache.jasper.runtime.HttpJspBase {\n"); javaSource.append(" public void _jspService(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response) throws Exception {\n"); javaSource.append(" JspWriter out = pageContext.getOut();\n"); for (String line : jspText.split("\\r?\\n")) { line = line.trim(); if (line.startsWith("<%--") && line.endsWith("--%>")) { continue; } else if (line.startsWith("<%=") && line.endsWith("%>")) { String expr = line.substring(3, line.length() - 2).trim(); javaSource.append(" out.print(").append(expr).append(");\n"); } else if (line.startsWith("<%") && line.endsWith("%>")) { String stmt = line.substring(2, line.length() - 2).trim(); javaSource.append(" ").append(stmt).append("\n"); } else if (!line.isBlank()) { javaSource.append(" out.write(\"").append(line.replace("\"", "\\\"")).append("\\n\");\n"); } } javaSource.append(" }\n}"); return javaSource.toString(); } public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("=== Jasper JSP Translation Simulator ==="); String sampleJsp = """ <%@ page contentType="text/html" %> <%-- User Greeting Banner --%>

Welcome to Java Handbook

<% String user = request.getParameter("name"); %>

Hello, <%= user != null ? user : "Guest" %>

"""; System.out.println("Generated Servlet Source (_jspService):"); String generated = translateJspSnippet(sampleJsp); System.out.println(generated); System.out.println("JSP translation simulation completed successfully."); } } ``` --- #### Example 2: Packaged Live JSP Template (Realistic) ```jsp <%@ page contentType="text/html;charset=UTF-8" language="java" %> JSP Translation Demo

Jakarta Pages 3.1 Live Translation

Server Time: <%= new java.util.Date() %>

Thread Handling Request: <%= Thread.currentThread().getName() %>

``` **Expected HTTP Response Output (`GET /hello.jsp`):** ```http HTTP/1.1 200 OK Content-Type: text/html;charset=UTF-8 JSP Translation Demo

Jakarta Pages 3.1 Live Translation

Server Time: Wed Nov 17 21:00:00 UTC 2026

Thread Handling Request: http-nio-8080-exec-3

``` --- ### 5. Step-by-Step Execution Trace 1. **Request Ingress**: Client requests `GET /hello.jsp`. 2. **Translation Verification**: Tomcat checks `$CATALINA_BASE/work/Catalina/localhost/handbook/` for `hello_jsp.class`. - If missing or if `hello.jsp` file timestamp is newer, Jasper translates the JSP into Java source code and compiles it with `javac`. 3. **Servlet Instantiation**: Tomcat loads `hello_jsp.class` into memory and invokes `jspInit()`. 4. **Service Dispatch**: Worker thread invokes `_jspService(req, resp)`, executing the embedded Java statements and writing HTML text to `out`. 5. **Caching**: Subsequent requests skip translation and compilation entirely, executing the cached in-memory servlet with high performance. --- ### 6. Common Mistakes & Gotchas #### Mistake 1: Expecting JSP modifications to apply if compilation fails *Why it fails*: If a syntax error is introduced into a JSP (e.g. mismatched brackets), Jasper fails compilation and returns HTTP 500. *The Fix*: Inspect Tomcat's `$CATALINA_HOME/logs/catalina.out` for the exact line number of the generated `.java` file. #### Mistake 2: Writing business logic and database queries directly in JSP *Why it fails*: Mixing SQL queries and business loops inside JSP leads to unmaintainable spaghetti code and violates MVC architecture. *The Fix*: Keep JSPs strictly as presentation views; perform all database queries inside Servlet Controllers and forward data via request attributes. --- ### 7. Best Practices - **Precompile JSPs for Production**: Use the Apache Tomcat JspC tool or Maven `jasper-maven-plugin` to precompile all JSPs at build time. This eliminates first-request latency spikes. - **Store Internal JSPs inside `WEB-INF/`**: Prevents users from directly executing templates without going through controlling servlets. --- ### 8. Version Notes - **JSP 1.0 (1999)**: Initial Sun Microsystems release. - **JSP 2.0 (Java EE 1.4)**: Introduced Expression Language (EL) and tag files. - **Jakarta Pages 3.1 (Jakarta EE 10)**: Modern namespace migration to `jakarta.servlet.jsp.*`. --- ### 9. Summary Cheat Sheet: JSP Lifecycle Stages | Stage | Triggered By | Output | Purpose | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Translation** | First request or build-time precompile | `.java` source file | Converts template tags into Java statements | | **Compilation** | Jasper compiler (`javac`) | `.class` bytecode | Generates executable servlet class | | **Initialization** | Container class loading | `jspInit()` hook | One-time startup initialization | | **Execution** | Every client HTTP request | `_jspService(req, resp)` | Generates dynamic response markup | | **Destruction** | Server shutdown / undeploy | `jspDestroy()` hook | Releases resources before unloading | --- ### 10. Exercises with Hidden Solutions #### Exercise 1: Spot the Bug (First-Request Performance Lag) Why do high-traffic enterprise applications experience latency spikes on the very first request to newly deployed JSPs?
View Solution ``` Cause: By default, Tomcat compiles JSPs lazily on the first incoming request. Translating text to .java and launching javac to produce bytecode takes 200ms to 2000ms. Fix: Precompile all JSPs during the build process using the Maven jasper plugin or configure Tomcat's org.apache.jasper.servlet.JspServlet load-on-startup in web.xml. ```
#### Exercise 2: Hands-on Implementation (JSP Comment vs HTML Comment) Explain the difference between `` and `<%-- JSP Comment --%>` in terms of network transmission.
View Solution ``` 1. <%-- JSP Comment --%>: Stripped during the Translation phase by Jasper. It NEVER appears in the generated Java servlet source or client HTML. 2. : Treated as static template text. It is written to out.write() and transmitted across the network to the browser DOM. ```
#### Exercise 3: Real-World Architecture (Precompilation in Docker) Why is JSP precompilation mandatory when deploying lightweight Docker containers without a full JDK installed?
View Solution ``` Tomcat's Jasper compiler requires a Java compiler (javac) to compile translated .java files. Minimal production Docker images (like JRE or distroless runtimes) do not contain javac. Precompiling JSPs into .class files at build time allows running web applications on minimal JRE runtimes without a JDK. ```
--- ### 11. Official Sources - [Jakarta Pages Specification 3.1](https://jakarta.ee/specifications/pages/3.1/) — Jakarta EE - [Apache Tomcat 10.1 Documentation: Jasper 2 JSP Engine](https://tomcat.apache.org/tomcat-10.1-doc/jasper-howto.html) — Apache Tomcat

# JSP Syntax Elements: Directives, Scriptlets & Expressions ### 1. What It Is and Why It Exists To provide dynamic functionality, Jakarta Pages defines a concise set of syntax delimiters that tell the Jasper compiler how to handle different segments of a `.jsp` file. Each element instructs Jasper where to place the code in the generated servlet: 1. **Directives (`<%@ ... %>`)**: Messages to the JSP container that apply globally to the page (page encoding, imported Java packages, tag libraries, static file inclusion). 2. **Declarations (`<%! ... %>`)**: Class-level variables and methods placed **outside** the `_jspService()` method directly into the generated servlet class body. 3. **Scriptlets (`<% ... %>`)**: Java statements executed sequentially **inside** the `_jspService()` method on every request. 4. **Expressions (`<%= ... %>`)**: Java expressions evaluated and automatically converted to text passed to `out.print()`. No trailing semicolon is permitted. 5. **JSP Comments (`<%-- ... --%>`)**: Server-side comments ignored during compilation. **Real-World Analogy:** Imagine filling out a government tax form: - Directives (`<%@ %>`) are the fine-print instructions at the top: language rules and which currency is used. - Declarations (`<%! %>`) are the permanent account numbers printed on the stationery. - Scriptlets (`<% %>`) are the calculations you perform on scrap paper. - Expressions (`<%= %>`) are the final calculated numbers written into the official answer boxes. --- ### 2. Prerequisites - **JSP Architecture & Translation (Topic 74)**: Understanding how Jasper transforms syntax tags into `_jspService()`. --- ### 3. Syntax Breakdown | Syntax Element | Delimiter | Where Placed in Generated Servlet | Typical Usage | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Page Directive** | `<%@ page ... %>` | Class imports and container headers | `<%@ page import="java.util.List" %>` | | **Include Directive** | `<%@ include file="..." %>` | Translation-time text merger | Merges static header/footer before compile | | **Declaration** | `<%! ... %>` | Class level (outside `_jspService`) | `<%! private int counter = 0; %>` | | **Scriptlet** | `<% ... %>` | Local statements inside `_jspService` | `<% String id = request.getParameter("id"); %>` | | **Expression** | `<%= ... %>` | Wrapped in `out.print(...)` | `<%= Math.round(price) %>` (No semicolon!) | | **JSP Comment** | `<%-- ... --%>` | Stripped entirely | Developer notes hidden from client | --- ### 4. Runnable Code Examples #### Example 1: Syntax Elements Live Demonstration (Basic) Demonstrates class declarations, local scriptlets, expressions, and directives. ```jsp <%@ page contentType="text/html;charset=UTF-8" language="java" import="java.time.LocalTime" %> <%! // Declaration: Becomes a field in the servlet class (Shared across threads!) private int globalPageViews = 0; private synchronized int incrementViews() { return ++globalPageViews; } %> JSP Syntax Breakdown

Jakarta Pages Syntax Demonstration

<%-- JSP Server-Side Comment --%> <% // Scriptlet: Local variable inside _jspService() (Thread-safe) String clientIp = request.getRemoteAddr(); LocalTime now = LocalTime.now(); int views = incrementViews(); %>

Client IP Address: <%= clientIp %>

Current Time: <%= now %>

Total Page Hits (All Users): <%= views %>

``` **Expected HTTP Response Output:** ```http HTTP/1.1 200 OK Content-Type: text/html;charset=UTF-8 JSP Syntax Breakdown

Jakarta Pages Syntax Demonstration

Client IP Address: 127.0.0.1

Current Time: 21:05:30.142

Total Page Hits (All Users): 1

``` --- #### Example 2: Static Include Directive vs Dynamic Include (Realistic) Demonstrates translation-time inclusion (`<%@ include %>`) for static components vs request-time inclusion (``). ```jsp <%@ page contentType="text/html;charset=UTF-8" %> Modular Layout Demo <%-- Static Translation-time include: Inlines file BEFORE compilation --%> <%@ include file="/WEB-INF/fragments/header.html" %>

Main Product Catalog Content

<% String[] categories = {"Hardware", "Software", "Cloud"}; for (String cat : categories) { %>
<%= cat %>
<% } %>
<%-- Dynamic Request-time include: Dispatches at runtime --%> ``` --- ### 5. Step-by-Step Execution Trace 1. **Compilation**: Jasper inspects `<%! ... %>` declarations and places `globalPageViews` as an instance field of `syntax_elements_jsp`. 2. **Page Directive Processing**: Jasper imports `java.time.LocalTime` and configures `response.setContentType("text/html;charset=UTF-8")`. 3. **Service Execution**: When `_jspService()` executes: - Evaluates `<% ... %>` scriptlets, creating local method variables `clientIp` and `now` on the thread stack. - Evaluates `<%= ... %>` expressions, converting the returned object to a String and calling `out.print()`. 4. **HTML Output**: The generated markup streams across the TCP connection to the user's browser. --- ### 6. Common Mistakes & Gotchas #### Mistake 1: Placing a semicolon inside an Expression (`<%= ... %>`) ```jsp <%-- WRONG: Throws compilation error! --%>

User: <%= user.getName(); %>

<%-- CORRECT: Expressions must NOT have trailing semicolons! --%>

User: <%= user.getName() %>

``` *Why it fails*: Jasper wraps expressions directly inside `out.print(...)`. If you add a semicolon, it translates to `out.print(user.getName(););`, which is invalid Java syntax. #### Mistake 2: Storing user-specific state in Declarations (`<%! ... %>`) ```jsp <%-- CATASTROPHIC RACE CONDITION! --%> <%! private String currentUser; %> <% currentUser = request.getParameter("user"); %> ``` *Why it fails*: Declarations create class instance fields. Remember that the container creates **only ONE instance** of the translated servlet shared across all concurrent users. Modifying declaration fields causes thread cross-contamination. *The Fix*: Always declare variables in scriptlets (`<% ... %>`) so they remain thread-safe local stack variables. --- ### 7. Best Practices - **Prefer Expression Language (EL) over Scriptlets**: Modern Jakarta EE development discourages raw `<% ... %>` scriptlets in favor of `${...}` and JSTL tags. - **Always Declare Page Encoding**: Always place `<%@ page contentType="text/html;charset=UTF-8" %>` at line 1 of every JSP. --- ### 8. Version Notes - **JSP 1.2**: Scriptlets, declarations, and expressions established. - **JSP 2.0**: Discouraged scriptlets in favor of Expression Language (EL). - **Jakarta Pages 3.1**: Scriptlet support retained for backward compatibility; pure EL recommended. --- ### 9. Summary Cheat Sheet: JSP Elements Syntax | Tag Syntax | Name | Semicolon Allowed? | Scope | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | `<%@ page ... %>` | Directive | No | Page-wide translation settings | | `<%! ... %>` | Declaration | **Yes** | Class instance scope (Shared across all threads) | | `<% ... %>` | Scriptlet | **Yes** | Method local scope (`_jspService`) | | `<%= ... %>` | Expression | **NO** | Evaluated parameter to `out.print()` | | `<%-- ... --%>` | JSP Comment | No | Completely stripped by compiler | --- ### 10. Exercises with Hidden Solutions #### Exercise 1: Spot the Bug (Semicolon in Expression) Why does this JSP fail to compile with Jasper error "Syntax error on token ';', invalid Expression"? ```jsp

Hello <%= request.getParameter("name"); %>

```
View Solution ```jsp // Cause: Semicolons are forbidden in expressions (<%= %>). // Translated code becomes: out.print(request.getParameter("name");); // Fix: Remove the semicolon:

Hello <%= request.getParameter("name") %>

```
#### Exercise 2: Hands-on Implementation (Safe Declaration Helper) Write a declaration element defining a helper method `formatPrice(double val)` that formats a number to two decimal places.
View Solution ```jsp <%! public String formatPrice(double price) { return String.format("$%.2f", price); } %>

Discounted Total: <%= formatPrice(49.956) %>

```
#### Exercise 3: Real-World Architecture (Static vs Dynamic Include) When should you use `<%@ include file="..." %>` vs ``?
View Solution ``` 1. <%@ include file="..." %> (Static / Translation-time): - Merges file contents verbatim BEFORE compilation. - Ideal for static HTML snippets, shared variable declarations, or taglib directives. - Faster execution because it compiles into a single unified servlet class. 2. (Dynamic / Request-time): - Invocations are dispatched via RequestDispatcher.include() at runtime. - Target page is compiled as an independent servlet. - Ideal for dynamic pages that change frequently or take runtime request parameters. ```
--- ### 11. Official Sources - [Jakarta Pages Specification 3.1: Chapter 1 Core Syntax](https://jakarta.ee/specifications/pages/3.1/) — Jakarta EE - [Apache Tomcat Documentation: JSP Syntax Reference](https://tomcat.apache.org/tomcat-10.1-doc/index.html) — Apache Tomcat

# JSP Implicit Objects & Standard Actions ### 1. What It Is and Why It Exists When writing scriptlets or expressions inside a JSP, you do not need to manually instantiate or declare request and response objects. The Jasper engine automatically declares **9 Implicit Objects** at the very beginning of the translated `_jspService()` method. In addition to implicit objects, the specification provides **JSP Standard Actions (``)**: built-in XML tags that manipulate JavaBeans, dynamically include external templates, forward control, and handle plugin applets without writing raw Java scriptlets. **Real-World Analogy:** Imagine walking into a fully equipped modern kitchen (**`_jspService()`**). You do not need to build a stove, bring your own running water, or wire electrical outlets from scratch; the nine essential kitchen appliances (**implicit objects**) are already plugged in, pre-calibrated, and ready for you to use. Standard actions are like automated kitchen buttons (e.g. "Auto-Clean" or "Timer Preset"). --- ### 2. Prerequisites - **JSP Architecture & Translation (Topic 74)**: Understanding how the translated `_jspService()` method is structured. - **Request and Response Processing (Topic 67)**: Working with `HttpServletRequest` and `HttpServletResponse`. --- ### 3. Syntax Breakdown #### 3.1 The 9 JSP Implicit Objects | Implicit Object | Java Type | Scope | Description | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **`request`** | `jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletRequest` | Request | Incoming request parameters, headers, cookies, and streams | | **`response`** | `jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletResponse` | Page | Outgoing headers, status codes, and redirect logic | | **`out`** | `jakarta.servlet.jsp.JspWriter` | Page | Buffered character output stream writing to the client | | **`session`** | `jakarta.servlet.http.HttpSession` | Session | Conversational user memory (only if `<%@ page session="true" %>`) | | **`application`** | `jakarta.servlet.ServletContext` | Application | Global application scope shared by all users and servlets | | **`config`** | `jakarta.servlet.ServletConfig` | Page | Servlet initialization parameters for this JSP page | | **`pageContext`** | `jakarta.servlet.jsp.PageContext` | Page | Central hub providing access to all 4 scopes and other implicit objects | | **`page`** | `java.lang.Object` (`this`) | Page | Reference to the current translated servlet instance | | **`exception`** | `java.lang.Throwable` | Page | Available only in error pages (`<%@ page isErrorPage="true" %>`) | #### 3.2 The 4 Attribute Scopes Objects can be stored and searched across four hierarchical scopes via `pageContext.findAttribute("name")`: 1. **Page Scope (`pageContext`)**: Accessible only within the current JSP page execution. 2. **Request Scope (`request`)**: Accessible across the current HTTP request lifecycle (including forwards). 3. **Session Scope (`session`)**: Accessible across all requests from the same user browser session. 4. **Application Scope (`application`)**: Accessible globally across all users and pages in the web app. #### 3.3 Core JSP Standard Actions - **``**: Locates or instantiates a JavaBean in the specified scope. - **``**: Sets property values on a JavaBean via setters. - **``**: Calls getter and converts output to text. - **``**: Dynamically dispatches request-time inclusion. - **``**: Transfers request to another page or servlet. --- ### 4. Runnable Code Examples #### Example 1: Standard Actions with JavaBean (Basic) Demonstrates ``, ``, and `` for state encapsulation. ```jsp <%@ page contentType="text/html;charset=UTF-8" %> <%-- Instantiate UserProfileBean in request scope --%> JSP Implicit Objects & Standard Actions

JSP Implicit Objects & Standard Actions Demo

Session ID: <%= session.getId() %>

Context Path: <%= application.getContextPath() %>

User Bean: ()

``` **Expected HTTP Response Output:** ```http HTTP/1.1 200 OK Content-Type: text/html;charset=UTF-8 JSP Implicit Objects & Standard Actions

JSP Implicit Objects & Standard Actions Demo

Session ID: B4920FA8103CD911

Context Path: /handbook

User Bean: Duke (duke@oracle.com)

``` --- #### Example 2: Dynamic Page Forwarding with `` (Realistic) ```jsp <%@ page contentType="text/html;charset=UTF-8" %> <% String role = request.getParameter("role"); if ("admin".equalsIgnoreCase(role)) { %> <%-- Internal server-side forward to admin dashboard --%> <% } else { %>

Standard User Portal

Welcome to public access.

<% } %> ``` --- ### 5. Step-by-Step Execution Trace 1. **Compilation Step**: Jasper recognizes ``. 2. **Bytecode Translation**: Jasper emits Java code inside `_jspService()`: ```java com.handbook.web.UserProfileBean userBean = (com.handbook.web.UserProfileBean) request.getAttribute("userBean"); if (userBean == null) { userBean = new com.handbook.web.UserProfileBean(); request.setAttribute("userBean", userBean); } ``` 3. **Property Setter**: `` generates `userBean.setUsername("Duke")`. 4. **Execution**: The JavaBean properties are set and rendered cleanly without writing raw Java casts. --- ### 6. Common Mistakes & Gotchas #### Mistake 1: Missing zero-argument public constructor in JavaBean ```java public class UserProfileBean { // Missing public UserProfileBean() {}! public UserProfileBean(String name) { ... } } ``` *Why it fails*: `` uses reflection (`Class.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance()`) to instantiate beans. If no public zero-arg constructor exists, it throws `java.lang.InstantiationException`. *The Fix*: Always provide an explicit public zero-argument constructor in all JavaBeans. #### Mistake 2: Accessing `session` on pages with `session="false"` ```jsp <%@ page session="false" %>

ID: <%= session.getId() %>

<%-- Compilation error! --%> ``` *Why it fails*: When `session="false"` is set, Jasper does not declare the `session` implicit variable in `_jspService()`. *The Fix*: Set `<%@ page session="true" %>` (the default) or access sessions through `request.getSession(false)`. --- ### 7. Best Practices - **Use `pageContext.findAttribute("key")` for Scope-Agnostic Lookups**: Searches page $\rightarrow$ request $\rightarrow$ session $\rightarrow$ application scopes automatically. - **Prefer Standard Actions Over Raw Casts**: `` avoids ugly `(MyType) request.getAttribute()` casting in presentation files. --- ### 8. Version Notes - **JSP 1.1**: The 9 implicit objects formalized. - **JSP 2.0**: `` and `` actions introduced. - **Jakarta Pages 3.1**: Maintained 100% backward compatibility for all 9 implicit objects. --- ### 9. Summary Cheat Sheet: The 9 Implicit Objects | Variable | Class Interface | Scope | Primary Purpose | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | `request` | `HttpServletRequest` | Request | Headers, query params, form inputs | | `response` | `HttpServletResponse` | Page | Status codes, redirect, headers | | `out` | `JspWriter` | Page | HTML stream writing | | `session` | `HttpSession` | Session | User conversational state | | `application` | `ServletContext` | Application | Global application shared attributes | | `config` | `ServletConfig` | Page | JSP servlet init parameters | | `pageContext` | `PageContext` | Page | Unified access to all scopes & objects | | `page` | `Object` (`this`) | Page | Servlet instance reference | | `exception` | `Throwable` | Page | Caught error in error pages | --- ### 10. Exercises with Hidden Solutions #### Exercise 1: Spot the Bug (Missing Scope Attribute) Where does `` store the bean if the `scope` attribute is omitted?
View Solution ``` Answer: It defaults to "page" scope. Consequence: The cart will be destroyed as soon as the current page finishes rendering! Fix: Specify scope="session": ```
#### Exercise 2: Hands-on Implementation (Application Scope Counter) Write a JSP snippet that retrieves an integer counter from `application` scope, increments it, and prints it.
View Solution ```jsp <% synchronized(application) { Integer visits = (Integer) application.getAttribute("totalVisits"); visits = (visits == null) ? 1 : visits + 1; application.setAttribute("totalVisits", visits); out.println("Total Global Visits: " + visits); } %> ```
#### Exercise 3: Real-World Architecture (PageContext Unified Lookup) In what exact order does `pageContext.findAttribute("user")` search the four web scopes?
View Solution ``` The lookup searches from narrowest scope to broadest scope: 1. Page scope (pageContext) 2. Request scope (request) 3. Session scope (session) 4. Application scope (application / ServletContext) Returns null if not found in any scope. ```
--- ### 11. Official Sources - [Jakarta Pages Specification 3.1: Chapter 2 Implicit Objects](https://jakarta.ee/specifications/pages/3.1/) — Jakarta EE - [Apache Tomcat 10.1 Documentation: PageContext API](https://tomcat.apache.org/tomcat-10.1-doc/jspapi/jakarta/servlet/jsp/PageContext.html) — Apache Tomcat

shortDescription: Write scriptlet-free web views: master Expression Language (${...}) property resolution, null-safety, and JSTL core tags (<c:forEach>, <c:if>, <c:choose>, <c:out>).
prerequisites: Topic 75: JSP Syntax Elements: Directives, Scriptlets & Expressions
Topic 76: JSP Implicit Objects & Standard Actions
markdownContent:
# Expression Language (EL) & JSTL Core Tags ### 1. What It Is and Why It Exists Early versions of JSP were plagued by Java scriptlets (`<% ... %>`). Mixing Java control flow (`for`, `if`, `try/catch`) with HTML produced unreadable, fragile markup that was difficult for frontend web designers to edit and prone to `NullPointerException` crashes. To modernize web presentation, the Jakarta EE community introduced two complementary standards: 1. **Jakarta Expression Language (EL) (`${...}`)**: A concise expression syntax designed to access JavaBeans, collections, maps, and scoped attributes with **automatic null-safety** (expressions evaluating to `null` render as empty strings rather than throwing `NullPointerException`). 2. **Jakarta Standard Tag Library (JSTL Core ``)**: Standard XML-style tags that replace raw Java loops (``), conditional checks (``, ``), variable declarations (``), and XSS-safe output (``). Together, EL and JSTL allow building dynamic web templates with **zero raw Java scriptlets**. **Real-World Analogy:** Imagine reading a magazine template. Instead of an editor printing raw complex database formulas on the page, the template uses clean placeholders like `{{Subscriber.Name}}` and `{{Issue.Date}}`. The printing machine automatically fills in the blanks and gracefully prints nothing if a subscriber has no middle name, rather than stopping the printing press with a fatal error. --- ### 2. Prerequisites - **JSP Implicit Objects & Scopes (Topic 76)**: Understanding the 4 attribute scopes (page, request, session, application). - **OOP Encapsulation & JavaBeans (Topic 19)**: Understanding getter naming conventions (`getName()` $\rightarrow$ `${bean.name}`). --- ### 3. Syntax Breakdown #### 3.1 Expression Language (EL) Fundamentals ```jsp <%-- Accessing JavaBean property (Calls user.getUsername()) --%> ${user.username} <%-- Accessing Map entry (${map['key'] or ${map.key}) --%> ${sessionScope.cart['itemCount']} <%-- Accessing List / Array index --%> ${products[0].price} <%-- Safe Navigation & Empty Check --%> ${empty cart ? 'Your cart is empty' : 'Items ready for checkout'} <%-- Ternary Conditional Operator --%> ${user.active ? 'Active Member' : 'Suspended'} ``` #### 3.2 Key EL Implicit Objects - **`${pageScope}`**, **`${requestScope}`**, **`${sessionScope}`**, **`${applicationScope}`**: Maps to specific attribute scopes. - **`${param}`** and **`${paramValues}`**: Maps to HTTP query parameters (`${param.id}`). - **`${header}`** and **`${headerValues}`**: Maps to HTTP request headers (`${header['User-Agent']}`). - **`${cookie}`**: Maps to HTTP cookies (`${cookie.theme.value}`). - **`${initParam}`**: Maps to context initialization parameters in `web.xml`. #### 3.3 Core JSTL Tag Library (`<%@ taglib prefix="c" uri="jakarta.tags.core" %>`) - **``**: Outputs value with **automatic HTML entity escaping** (defends against XSS). - **``**: Binds a variable into a scope. - **``**: Conditional rendering. - **`......`**: `switch / if-else` equivalent. - **``**: Loops over collections and arrays. --- ### 4. Runnable Code Examples #### Example 1: Jakarta Expression Language Evaluator Demo (Basic) Demonstrates programmatic EL resolution against JavaBeans, Scoped Maps, and empty checks. ```java package com.handbook.web; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; public class ExpressionLanguageEvaluatorDemo { public static Object resolveElProperty(Object target, String property) throws Exception { if (target instanceof Map map) { return map.get(property); } String getterName = "get" + Character.toUpperCase(property.charAt(0)) + property.substring(1); return target.getClass().getMethod(getterName).invoke(target); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { System.out.println("=== Jakarta Expression Language (EL) Evaluator ==="); UserProfileBean user = new UserProfileBean("jduke", "duke@oracle.com", 1500, true); System.out.println("Resolving EL expressions against JavaBean:"); System.out.println(" ${user.username} -> " + resolveElProperty(user, "username")); System.out.println(" ${user.email} -> " + resolveElProperty(user, "email")); System.out.println(" ${user.loyaltyPoints} -> " + resolveElProperty(user, "loyaltyPoints")); Map sessionScope = new HashMap<>(); sessionScope.put("theme", "VS Code Dark+"); sessionScope.put("cartItems", List.of("Spring Boot Book", "Java Concurrency In Practice")); System.out.println("\nResolving EL expressions against Scoped Maps:"); System.out.println(" ${sessionScope.theme} -> " + resolveElProperty(sessionScope, "theme")); List items = (List) resolveElProperty(sessionScope, "cartItems"); System.out.println(" ${empty sessionScope.cartItems} -> " + (items == null || items.isEmpty())); System.out.println(" ${sessionScope.cartItems[0]} -> " + items.get(0)); System.out.println("\nExpression Language evaluation completed successfully."); } } ``` **Execution Output:** ``` === Jakarta Expression Language (EL) Evaluator === Resolving EL expressions against JavaBean: ${user.username} -> jduke ${user.email} -> duke@oracle.com ${user.loyaltyPoints} -> 1500 Resolving EL expressions against Scoped Maps: ${sessionScope.theme} -> VS Code Dark+ ${empty sessionScope.cartItems} -> false ${sessionScope.cartItems[0]} -> Spring Boot Book Expression Language evaluation completed successfully. ``` --- #### Example 2: Clean JSTL Product Catalog View (Realistic) ```jsp <%@ page contentType="text/html;charset=UTF-8" %> <%@ taglib prefix="c" uri="jakarta.tags.core" %> Product Catalog

Store Products

<%-- Safe text output with XSS escaping --%>

Logged in as:

No products available in this category.
#ProductPriceStatus
${loop.count} $${p.price} In Stock Sold Out
``` --- ### 5. Step-by-Step Execution Trace 1. **EL Evaluation**: The EL resolver encounters `${user.username}`. 2. **Scope Traversal**: Searches `pageScope` $\rightarrow$ `requestScope` $\rightarrow$ `sessionScope` $\rightarrow$ `applicationScope`. Finds the `user` attribute in `requestScope`. 3. **Property Extraction**: Discovers JavaBean getter method `getUsername()` via reflection and invokes it. 4. **Null Safety**: If `user` or `username` is `null`, the expression evaluates to empty text `""` without throwing a `NullPointerException`. 5. **JSTL Loop Iteration**: `` evaluates `${products}`, wraps it in a standard iterator, and loops once for each element, binding the current item to page-scoped variable `p`. --- ### 6. Common Mistakes & Gotchas #### Mistake 1: Using legacy JCP URI for JSTL in Jakarta EE 10 ```jsp <%-- WRONG IN JAKARTA EE 10 / TOMCAT 10.1: --%> <%@ taglib prefix="c" uri="http://java.sun.com/jsp/jstl/core" %> <%-- CORRECT IN JAKARTA EE 10: --%> <%@ taglib prefix="c" uri="jakarta.tags.core" %> ``` *Why it fails*: Jakarta EE 10 updated the standard taglib URI from `http://java.sun.com/jsp/jstl/core` to `jakarta.tags.core`. Using the old URI causes Jasper to fail with "Tag library not found". #### Mistake 2: Missing getter method for EL properties ```jsp

Total: ${order.totalPrice}

<%-- PropertyNotFoundException! --%> ``` *Why it fails*: EL requires strict JavaBean getter conventions. If the class declares `double totalPrice;` but forgot `public double getTotalPrice()`, EL throws `PropertyNotFoundException`. *The Fix*: Always declare public getters matching JavaBean specifications. --- ### 7. Best Practices - **Strictly Disallow Scriptlets**: You can enforce a scriptlet-free policy in `web.xml`: ```xml *.jsp true ``` - **Always Output User Input via ``**: Prevents Reflected XSS attacks by automatically converting `<`, `>`, and `&` to HTML entity equivalents. --- ### 8. Version Notes - **EL 1.0**: Introduced in JSP 2.0. - **Jakarta EL 5.0 (Jakarta EE 10)**: Standalone specification; added lambda expressions in EL, method invocations with arguments `${calc.multiply(a, b)}`, and stream operations. - **Jakarta Standard Tag Library 3.0**: Migrated taglib URI to `jakarta.tags.core`. --- ### 9. Summary Cheat Sheet: Core JSTL Tags | JSTL Tag | Attribute | Purpose | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | `` | `value="${expr}"` | Escapes HTML entities and renders output | | `` | `var="x" value="..." scope="..."` | Binds variable to specified scope | | `` | `var="x" scope="..."` | Removes variable from scope | | `` | `test="${condition}"` | Simple conditional execution | | `` | Parent container | `switch / if-else` structure | | `` | `test="${condition}"` | `case / if` branch inside `` | | `` | Default branch | `default / else` branch inside `` | | `` | `items="${coll}" var="x"` | Iterates over arrays, lists, maps, collections | --- ### 10. Exercises with Hidden Solutions #### Exercise 1: Spot the Bug (EL Null Check) Why is `test="${cart != null && cart.size() > 0}"` worse than `test="${not empty cart}"` in Expression Language?
View Solution ``` The "empty" operator in EL is specifically designed for collections: 1. It automatically checks if cart is null. 2. If non-null, it checks if the collection, array, or string is empty (size == 0 or length == 0). 3. Using ${not empty cart} is concise, idiomatic, and completely immune to NullPointerException. ```
#### Exercise 2: Hands-on Implementation (Safe User Welcome Banner) Write a JSP snippet using JSTL that displays `

Welcome, [Username]!

` if logged in, or `Please Sign In` if anonymous, with complete XSS escaping.
View Solution ```jsp <%@ taglib prefix="c" uri="jakarta.tags.core" %>

Welcome, !

 Please Sign In ```
#### Exercise 3: Real-World Architecture (Bracket vs Dot Operator) When is `${user['first-name']}` required instead of `${user.first-name}`?
View Solution ``` 1. When property names contain hyphens or special characters: ${user.first-name} is evaluated as subtraction (${user.first minus name})! Bracket notation ${user['first-name']} treats the property name as an exact literal string key. 2. When property names are dynamic: ${user[propertyName]}. ```
--- ### 11. Official Sources - [Jakarta Expression Language Specification 5.0](https://jakarta.ee/specifications/expression-language/5.0/) — Jakarta EE - [Jakarta Standard Tag Library Specification 3.0](https://jakarta.ee/specifications/tags/3.0/) — Jakarta EE

# Custom JSP Tag Libraries ### 1. What It Is and Why It Exists While the Jakarta Standard Tag Library (JSTL) covers universal programming operations (loops, conditionals, URL formatting), real-world enterprise applications have specialized domain requirements: - Formatting localized monetary values and tax breakdowns. - Rendering complex navigation menus based on role permissions. - Masking sensitive personal data (e.g. credit card `****-****-****-1234`). - Rendering reusable UI widgets and interactive components. Rather than copying repetitive EL logic across hundreds of view files, the Jakarta Pages platform allows developers to create **Custom Tag Libraries**. A custom tag is an XML element backed by a Java class (extending `SimpleTagSupport`) and registered in a **Tag Library Descriptor (`.tld`)** XML file. **Real-World Analogy:** Imagine building a physical house. Standard JSTL tags are basic construction materials like 2x4 wooden studs, common nails, and drywall sheets. Custom Tag Libraries are pre-fabricated modular components—such as a custom bay window unit or an engineered spiral staircase—manufactured once in a factory and dropped cleanly into multiple rooms with a single installation step. --- ### 2. Prerequisites - **JSP Architecture & Translation (Topic 74)**: Understanding how the container compiles tags into Java method calls. - **Expression Language (EL) & JSTL (Topic 77)**: Understanding taglib directives and attribute passing. --- ### 3. Syntax Breakdown #### 3.1 The Simple Tag Handler Lifecycle (`SimpleTagSupport`) The `jakarta.servlet.jsp.tagext.SimpleTagSupport` base class provides a clean, streamlined lifecycle for authoring custom tags: ```java package jakarta.servlet.jsp.tagext; public class SimpleTagSupport implements SimpleTag { public void setJspContext(JspContext pc) { ... } public void setParent(JspTag parent) { ... } public void setJspBody(JspFragment jspBody) { ... } // THE CORE HOOK OVERRIDDEN BY DEVELOPERS: public void doTag() throws JspException, IOException { ... } } ``` 1. **Container creates an instance** of the tag handler. 2. **`setJspContext()`** supplies the `PageContext`. 3. **Setter methods** are invoked for each declared tag attribute. 4. **`doTag()`** executes; writes custom output to `getJspContext().getOut()`. #### 3.2 The Tag Library Descriptor (`.tld`) Custom tags must be declared in an XML descriptor file placed inside `WEB-INF/` or `META-INF/`: ```xml 1.0 hb https://handbook.java/tags formatCurrency com.handbook.web.FormatCurrencyTag empty amount true true double ``` --- ### 4. Runnable Code Examples #### Example 1: Localized Currency Formatter Tag Handler (Basic) Demonstrates extending `SimpleTagSupport`, receiving typed attributes, and formatting currency. ```java package com.handbook.web; import jakarta.servlet.jsp.JspException; import jakarta.servlet.jsp.JspWriter; import jakarta.servlet.jsp.tagext.SimpleTagSupport; import java.io.IOException; import java.text.NumberFormat; import java.util.Locale; public class FormatCurrencyTag extends SimpleTagSupport { private double amount; private String currencyCode = "USD"; // Setters called automatically by container public void setAmount(double amount) { this.amount = amount; } public void setCurrencyCode(String currencyCode) { this.currencyCode = currencyCode; } @Override public void doTag() throws JspException, IOException { JspWriter out = getJspContext().getOut(); Locale locale = "EUR".equalsIgnoreCase(currencyCode) ? Locale.GERMANY : Locale.US; NumberFormat formatter = NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance(locale); out.print(formatter.format(amount)); } } ``` --- #### Example 2: Consuming Custom Tags in JSP (Realistic) ```jsp <%@ page contentType="text/html;charset=UTF-8" %> <%@ taglib prefix="hb" uri="https://handbook.java/tags" %> Custom Tag Demo

Custom Tag Currency Formatting

Product A Price:

Product B Price:

``` **Expected HTTP Response Output:** ```http HTTP/1.1 200 OK Content-Type: text/html;charset=UTF-8 Custom Tag Demo

Custom Tag Currency Formatting

Product A Price: $149.99

Product B Price: 129,50 €

``` --- ### 5. Step-by-Step Execution Trace 1. **Taglib Discovery**: Jasper parses `<%@ taglib prefix="hb" uri="https://handbook.java/tags" %>` and locates `handbook-tags.tld` inside `WEB-INF/tld/`. 2. **Class Lookup**: When encountering ``, Jasper identifies `com.handbook.web.FormatCurrencyTag`. 3. **Instantiation**: Inside translated `_jspService()`, a new `FormatCurrencyTag` instance is allocated. 4. **Attribute Injection**: Jasper invokes `tag.setAmount(149.99)` and `tag.setCurrencyCode("USD")`. 5. **Execution**: `tag.doTag()` runs, acquires the `JspWriter`, formats `$149.99`, and prints it directly to the socket response. --- ### 6. Common Mistakes & Gotchas #### Mistake 1: Missing `true` in `.tld` ```xml amount true ``` *Why it fails*: If `` (Runtime Expression Value) is omitted or `false`, passing an EL expression like `` throws a compilation error because Jasper treats the input as literal text rather than evaluating EL. *The Fix*: Always specify `true` on attributes meant to accept dynamic `${...}` values. #### Mistake 2: Storing state across invocations in tag handler fields *Why it fails*: If a tag handler instance is reused by the container (tag pooling), uncleared fields can leak data between different tag executions. *The Fix*: Ensure all fields are overwritten by setters or reset before `doTag()` completes. --- ### 7. Best Practices - **Use Tag Files (`.tag`) for UI Component Layouts**: For pure HTML/CSS component layouts, write `.tag` files in `WEB-INF/tags/` instead of compiled Java classes. - **Use Java Custom Tags for Heavy Computation**: Use Java classes (`SimpleTagSupport`) when custom formatting requires Java APIs (number formatting, encryption, database access). --- ### 8. Version Notes - **JSP 1.1**: Classic tag handlers (`TagSupport`, `BodyTagSupport`) introduced (verbose lifecycle). - **JSP 2.0**: Introduced `SimpleTagSupport` and Tag Files (`.tag`), simplifying custom tag development by 80%. - **Jakarta Pages 3.1 (Jakarta EE 10)**: Schema updated to `https://jakarta.ee/xml/ns/jakartaee/web-jsptaglibrary_3_0.xsd`. --- ### 9. Summary Cheat Sheet: Tag Library Descriptor XML Elements | TLD Element | Sub-elements | Purpose | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | `` | ``, ``, `` | Root container defining library metadata and unique URI | | `` | ``, ``, `` | Declares a single tag and its backing Java class | | `` | `empty`, `scriptless`, `tagdependent` | Declares whether tag accepts child markup | | `` | ``, ``, ``, `` | Declares a tag parameter and whether it accepts EL | --- ### 10. Exercises with Hidden Solutions #### Exercise 1: Spot the Bug (Static String Parsing) Why does `` print the literal string `"${errorMessage}"` on the browser rather than the actual message?
View Solution ``` Cause: The attribute definition in the .tld file lacks true. Without rtexprvalue set to true, the JSP compiler treats the value as literal text and does not invoke the EL resolver. Fix: Add true to the attribute definition in the TLD file. ```
#### Exercise 2: Hands-on Implementation (Masking Sensitive Credit Cards) Write a `doTag()` method in a `MaskCreditCardTag` that prints only the last 4 digits of a 16-digit card string, masking the first 12 with asterisks.
View Solution ```java public class MaskCreditCardTag extends SimpleTagSupport { private String cardNumber; public void setCardNumber(String cardNumber) { this.cardNumber = cardNumber; } @Override public void doTag() throws JspException, IOException { if (cardNumber == null || cardNumber.length() < 4) { getJspContext().getOut().print("****"); return; } String lastFour = cardNumber.substring(cardNumber.length() - 4); getJspContext().getOut().print("****-****-****-" + lastFour); } } ```
#### Exercise 3: Real-World Architecture (Body Content Types) What is the difference between `empty` and `scriptless`?
View Solution ``` 1. empty: The tag MUST NOT have any body content. It must be written as a self-closing tag () or have empty body (). 2. scriptless: The tag can contain body content including HTML, EL expressions (${...}), and other custom tags, but CANNOT contain raw Java scriptlets (<% %>). This is the standard for modern tags. ```
